title: Focal Loss for Dense Object Detection
venue: IEEE International Conference on Computer Vision (ICCV)

problem.summary: One-stage detectors sample the image densely and therefore see a huge foreground/background class imbalance during training; this imbalance, not architecture, is why one-stage detectors have trailed two-stage detectors in accuracy, since easy background negatives dominate the loss and gradients.
statements: One-stage detectors applied over dense samplings of locations, scales and aspect ratios have trailed the accuracy of two-stage detectors.
Extreme foreground-background class imbalance (e.g. 1:1000) encountered during training of dense detectors is the central cause of this accuracy gap.
Most evaluated locations are easy negatives that contribute no useful learning signal, and en masse they overwhelm training and can lead to degenerate models.
Prior remedies (hard negative mining, bootstrapping, OHEM, fixed positive/negative sampling ratios) are heuristics that discard or down-weight examples outside the loss itself.

evidence.quote: In contrast, one-stage detectors that are applied over a regular, dense sampling of possible object locations have the potential to be faster and simpler, but have trailed the accuracy of two-stage detectors thus far.
We discover that the extreme foreground-background class imbalance encountered during training of dense detectors is the central cause.
(1) training is inefficient as most locations are easy negatives that contribute no useful learning signal; (2) en masse, the easy negatives can overwhelm training and lead to degenerate models.
While similar sampling heuristics may also be applied, they are inefficient as the training procedure is still dominated by easily classified background examples.

background.summary: The paper builds on the two-stage R-CNN lineage (Selective Search proposals, RPN, FPN Faster R-CNN, OHEM) as the accuracy reference and on the one-stage line (OverFeat, YOLO, SSD, DSSD) as the speed reference. The claimed gap is that two-stage systems handle imbalance structurally via cascade and biased sampling, while one-stage systems had no comparably effective mechanism.

relatedWork.name: Faster R-CNN
relatedWork.relation: dominant two-stage framework that RPN integrated into a single convolution network
relatedWork.quote: Region Proposal Networks (RPN) integrated proposal generation with the second-stage classifier into a single convolution network, forming the Faster RCNN framework [28].

relatedWork.name: SSD / YOLO
relatedWork.relation: prior one-stage detectors tuned for speed whose accuracy trailed two-stage methods
relatedWork.quote: These detectors have been tuned for speed but their accuracy trails that of twostage methods.

relatedWork.name: OHEM
relatedWork.relation: prior hard-example selection technique used as the main training baseline; discards easy examples rather than down-weighting them
relatedWork.quote: Like the focal loss, OHEM puts more emphasis on misclassified examples, but unlike FL, OHEM completely discards easy examples.

relatedWork.name: FPN / RPN anchors
relatedWork.relation: RetinaNet reuses the anchor concept from RPN and feature pyramids from SSD and FPN
relatedWork.quote: the concept of ‘anchors’ introduced by RPN [28] and use of features pyramids as in SSD [22] and FPN [20]

relatedWork.name: R-CNN-like two-stage cascade
relatedWork.relation: how existing two-stage detectors address class imbalance, the mechanism focal loss replaces for one-stage training
relatedWork.quote: Class imbalance is addressed in R-CNN-like detectors by a two-stage cascade and sampling heuristics.

evidence.quote: SSD has a 10-20% lower AP, while YOLO focuses on an even more extreme speed/accuracy trade-off.

Recent work showed that two-stage detectors can be made fast simply by reducing input image resolution and the number of proposals, but one-stage methods trailed in accuracy even with a larger compute budget [17].

solution.summary: The focal loss modulates cross-entropy with a factor (1 − pt)^γ so that well-classified examples are sharply down-weighted (with an α-balanced variant used in practice), and RetinaNet is a deliberately simple one-stage FPN detector trained with this loss over all anchors, plus a prior-based bias initialization that stabilizes early training.
solution.approach: Reshape cross-entropy with a modulating factor (1 − pt)^γ (α-balanced in practice) that decays the loss of easy examples to zero, so training on all ~100k anchors is dominated by hard examples without any sampling heuristic.
components: focal loss FL(pt) = −αt(1 − pt)^γ log(pt) with γ = 2, α = 0.25 by default
ResNet + Feature Pyramid Network backbone with levels P3 through P7 (256 channels each)
classification subnet: four 3×3 conv layers plus a final 3×3 conv with KA sigmoid outputs, shared across pyramid levels
box regression subnet: same structure with 4A class-agnostic linear outputs
9 translation-invariant anchors per level (3 scales × 3 aspect ratios) with IoU 0.5/0.4 assignment
prior bias initialization b = −log((1 − π)/π) with π = 0.01 on the final classification layer
top-1k decoding per level, confidence threshold 0.05, NMS at 0.5

evidence.quote: We propose to address this class imbalance by reshaping the standard cross entropy loss such that it down-weights the loss assigned to well-classified examples.
we propose to reshape the loss function to down-weight easy examples and thus focus training on hard negatives.
RetinaNet is a single, unified network composed of a backbone network and two task-specific subnetworks.
the focal loss is applied to all ∼100k anchors in each sampled image

experiments.summary: All experiments are on COCO (trainval35k training, minival ablations, test-dev for headline results) with AP metrics, including sweeps over γ/α, anchor density, FL vs. α-balanced CE vs. OHEM, and speed/accuracy trade-offs across ResNet-50/101 and input scales 400-800.

evidence.quote: Our results show that when trained with the focal loss, RetinaNet is able to match the speed of previous one-stage detectors while surpassing the accuracy of all existing state-of-the-art two-stage detectors.
With γ = 2, FL yields a 2.9 AP improvement over the α-balanced CE loss.
Compared to existing one-stage methods, our approach achieves a healthy 5.9 point AP gap (39.1 vs. 33.2) with the closest competitor, DSSD [9], while also being faster, see Figure 2.
In contrast, the best setting for OHEM (no 1:3 ratio, batch size 128, nms of .5) achieves 32.8 AP.

limitations.summary: The work targets one-stage dense detectors rather than two-stage ones, top accuracy comes at roughly 5 fps, the fastest operating regimes are explicitly out of scope, and training without the special prior initialization diverges.
items: The high frame-rate regime is not addressed and would require special network design, which is declared beyond scope.
The best-accuracy configuration (about 40.8 AP) runs at roughly 198 ms, i.e. around 5 fps, so peak accuracy is not real-time.
Standard cross-entropy training without the prior bias initialization fails quickly by diverging, so the recipe depends on that initialization.
The analysis is limited to COCO bounding-box detection with an anchor-based, NMS-post-processed design.
Two-stage detectors do not need the proposed loss: they already control imbalance through the cascade and biased minibatch sampling.

evidence.quote: Addressing the high frame rate regime will likely require special network design, as in [27], and is beyond the scope of this work.
This fails quickly, with the network diverging during training.
Two-stage detectors are often trained with the cross entropy loss without use of α-balancing or our proposed loss.

futureDirections.direction: Design specialized architectures to operate in the very high frame-rate regime, which this work explicitly leaves open.
futureDirections.quote: Addressing the high frame rate regime will likely require special network design, as in [27], and is beyond the scope of this work.

futureDirections.direction: Generalize beyond the exact focal loss formula to any loss with similar down-weighting properties (as explored with FL* in the appendix).
futureDirections.quote: The exact form of the focal loss is not crucial.

futureDirections.direction: Adopt the stronger ResNeXt-101-FPN backbone reported after the main results to push accuracy further past 40 AP.
futureDirections.quote: Plugging in ResNeXt32x8d-101-FPN [38] as the RetinaNet backbone further improves results another 1.7 AP, surpassing 40 AP on COCO.

deploymentClaims: RetinaNet-101-600 runs in 122 ms per image versus 172 ms for the ResNet-101-FPN Faster R-CNN, both measured on an Nvidia M40 GPU.
RetinaNet-101-800 achieves 37.8 AP at 198 ms; RetinaNet-50-500 achieves 32.5 AP at 73 ms (COCO test-dev).
Training time ranges between 10 and 35 hours for the models in Table 1e, using 8 GPUs with synchronized SGD.
Code is released in the Detectron repository.

evidence.quote: Enabled by the focal loss, our simple one-stage RetinaNet detector outperforms all previous one-stage and two-stage detectors, including the best reported Faster R-CNN [28] system from [20].
while running at 5 fps, surpassing the previously best published single-model results from both one and two-stage detectors, see Figure 2.
